subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Introduction to Classroom Assessment and Basic Terms
The Cognitive Levels of Bloom's Taxonomy

subjective.topic: Introduction to Classroom Assessment and Basic Terms
subjective.question: Define classroom assessment. Also write the emerging points from its definitions.
subjective.answer: According to Palomba and Banta (1999), assessment is the systematic collection, review, and use of information about educational programs undertaken for the purpose of improving student learning and development. According to Huba and Freed (2000), assessment is the process of gathering and discussing information from multiple and diverse sources in order to develop an understanding of what students know and understand; the process culminates when assessment results are used to improve subsequent learning. The emerging points from these definitions are: (1) assessment is a systematic process in which circumstances, goals and planning are kept in mind — nothing takes place haphazardly; (2) information is gathered from different sources such as homework, exam papers, class tests and projects; (3) judgment is made about what has been achieved and what is still missing; (4) the judgment is made about a process or a product; and (5) the purpose of all this judgment is improvement. Assessment is like a bridge that connects the past (behind) as well as the future of the students.

subjective.topic: Introduction to Classroom Assessment and Basic Terms
subjective.question: Differentiate between measurement, testing, assessment and evaluation.
subjective.answer: Measurement refers to dimensions, quantity or weight; it is normally shown by using numbers and is always made with reference to some scale, e.g. measuring or weighing a box. Testing refers to the process of judging some ability or deciding about some ability, e.g. testing the ability for driving or testing IQ in a classroom. Assessment is a broader term which also includes measurement and testing; it is usually done with reference to some goals, e.g. assessing how firmly a student has learnt the hundred words assigned for the weekend. Evaluation is a complex process and the broadest term, including measurement, testing and assessment; all these together give the value of the product or process being assessed, and evaluation also provides the ground for improvement.

subjective.topic: Introduction to Classroom Assessment and Basic Terms
subjective.question: Why is modification or improvement called the basic purpose of assessment?
subjective.answer: The basic purpose of every assessment is to make changes; there is no use of assessment if improvements are not made. For example, a teacher develops a lesson plan, implements it in the classroom, and at the end it is evaluated. The purpose of evaluating it is modification and improvement. In the classroom context, information is gathered systematically from different sources (questioning, assignments, quizzes, exams), and the results always open grounds of improvement in teaching and learning; they can even be reviewed critically to make changes in syllabi, curriculum or policies at the policy-making level.

subjective.question: Differentiate between formative and summative assessment.
subjective.answer: Formative assessment is a type of testing in which a range of formal and informal assessment procedures is employed by teachers during the learning process in order to modify teaching and learning activities to improve student attainment. Its key points are: a range of formal and informal assessment, during the learning process, to modify teaching and learning, and to improve. Summative assessment, in contrast, refers to the assessment of participants and summarizes their development at a particular time; its focus is on the outcome of the program. Its key points are: assessment of participants, development at a particular time, and the outcome of a program.

subjective.question: Write a note on internal and external assessment with examples.
subjective.answer: Internal assessment is the process by which an organization assesses its policies and systems internally; it is carried out by the departments within the organization, and the employees themselves are skilled at managing it. External assessment involves an external organization or a consultancy firm to judge and monitor the organizational procedures and give an unbiased opinion for betterment. The focus is on the internal system versus external agencies; for example, a house exam conducted by the school itself is internal assessment, while a board exam conducted by an external board is external assessment.

subjective.question: Differentiate between process assessment and product assessment.
subjective.answer: Process assessment means the assessment of the process taking place, including the factors involved in it; the key words are 'during any process', for example, classroom proceedings while teaching and learning are going on. Product assessment means the assessment of the product at the end of some process; here achievement at the end, with reference to some goal, is important, for instance, the final grades of the students.

subjective.question: What is diagnostic assessment? In which fields has it been most helpful?
subjective.answer: Diagnostic assessment helps to diagnose the weak areas of learners; it looks for problem areas of a student during the learning process. It has normally been studied with reference to language learning, and it has been especially helpful in the language and mathematical fields, where it identifies the exact points at which the learner is facing difficulty so that remedial help can be planned.

subjective.question: Differentiate between norm-referenced and criterion-referenced assessment.
subjective.answer: A norm-referenced assessment makes judgments about people on the basis of scores and distributions of scores; for instance, the top 10 percent of the class are awarded first class and the next 15 percent second class. It has been the most common type of assessment used in education, though it does not give accurate and exact assessment — a student who fails in one year may well have passed in another. A criterion-referenced assessment makes judgments about performance rather than scores; it assesses the extent to which a student has received the performance outcomes of a subject, e.g. an oral presentation judged on criteria such as knowledge of subject material, ability to respond to questions, structure of presentation, use of audio/visual aids, pace, timing and delivery style. Norm-referenced is more common and has been in practice for years, whereas criterion-referenced is new and less practiced; criterion-referenced is closer to real-life situations.

subjective.question: Define reliability. Which procedures are used to attain reliability in assessment?
subjective.answer: Reliability refers to the extent to which assessment results are consistent; the assessment that maintains consistency in results is known as reliable. Carmines and Zeller (1979) define it as the extent to which a measurement instrument or procedure yields the same results on repeated trials. Unreliable results mean inconsistency, so we can trust results only if they are consistent. Different methods are used to attain reliability: the test-retest procedure, the alternative-test form procedure, the split-halves procedure and the internal consistency procedure.

subjective.question: Explain the test-retest procedure with its advantages and disadvantages.
subjective.answer: In the test-retest procedure, the same test is given two or more times to the same students; if the results are similar on both occasions, the assessment results are assumed to be reliable. Advantages: it has strong logical appeal because one is measuring more than once with the identical test, and one avoids the problem of developing more than one test. Disadvantages: events taking place between the two administrations may affect the results, persons might change, and students become more practiced the second time.

subjective.question: Write a note on the split-halves and internal consistency procedures of reliability.
subjective.answer: In the split-halves procedure, the same test is administered once, each half is graded separately, and the grades from each half are compared. Its advantages are that only one test needs to be developed and there is no maturation and no cueing; its disadvantage is the question of what the criterion of splitting the halves should be. In the internal consistency procedure, the same test is administered once and the score is based upon the average similarity of responses to the items; it evaluates the degree to which different test items that probe the same construct produce similar results. Its advantages are the same (one test, no maturation, no cueing), while its disadvantage is that scholars do not agree on the formula applied to calculate internal consistency.

subjective.question: What is the range of the reliability coefficient? How are its values interpreted?
subjective.answer: The value of the reliability coefficient ranges from 0 to 1.0. A coefficient of 0 means no reliability, while 1.0 means perfect reliability, which is hard to claim. If the coefficient is above 0.80, the test is said to have good reliability; if it is below 0.50, the test would not be considered a very reliable test.

subjective.question: Define validity and explain its different types in brief.
subjective.answer: Validity means how well a test measures what it is supposed to measure; an invalid test fails to measure what it is supposed to measure, e.g. a vocabulary test cannot be valid if it measures grammar ability. Its types are: (1) Face validity — whether the test appears to test what it is supposed to test, e.g. a drawing test should contain figures and a multiple choice question must have options. (2) Content validity — it refers to the contents a test is supposed to measure, i.e. the test items should represent the contents of the course. (3) Construct validity — it refers to the construction of the test, i.e. how aptly the contents of the course are covered in the question paper. (4) Criterion-related validity — how much a test can measure some performance with reference to some defined standards. (5) Predictive validity — how much a test can predict future performance with reference to some defined standard.

subjective.question: What is the link between reliability and validity?
subjective.answer: Reliability and validity are related concepts. Reliability is the consistency of results, while validity is how well a test measures what it is supposed to measure. A test cannot be reliable if it is not valid; we can trust the results of an assessment only when they have been attained from a valid and consistent testing process, which is the evidence of an accurate system of assessment.

subjective.question: What is bias in assessment? Explain unfairness and offensiveness as its types.
subjective.answer: Bias is an inclination for or prejudice against one person or group, especially in a way that is considered to be unfair; it is the systematic unfair treatment of a particular group of individuals. Unfairness means that someone's right is denied due to like or dislike; in assessment it is normally associated with teachers. It creates mistrust among the stakeholders of assessment, affects the whole process and questions the standards of assessment. Offensiveness means using such language in a question, or such an attitude, that may offend someone. Offensiveness not only deforms the image of the teacher but also proves that the assessment system is not reliable.

subjective.question: Which measures can be taken to eliminate bias from assessment?
subjective.answer: The measures to eliminate bias include: striving for diversity in test-development staffing and training test developers and scorers to be aware of the potential for cultural, linguistic and socioeconomic bias; having test material reviewed by experts and trained persons; screening for and eliminating items, references and terms that are more likely to be offensive to certain groups; and using multiple assessment measures to determine academic achievement and progress. In addition, giving equal opportunities to all — equality in time, in opportunities and equal standards for all in grading — reduces biasness and creates a harmony that leads towards equity, and physically challenged students must be facilitated in a balanced way.

subjective.question: What is an assessment tool? Describe the main tools of assessment in brief.
subjective.answer: An assessment tool is a method of collecting information about a learner's performance and understanding about a certain topic. The main tools are: Observation — a process by which a teacher observes one or more class sessions and records the practices and student actions. Interview — a formal face-to-face meeting normally designed with the purpose of assessment. Projects — an individual or collaborative enterprise that is carefully planned to achieve a particular aim, with the purpose of assessment. Diaries — a daily record, usually private, of the writer's own experiences, observations, feelings and attitudes, used here for assessment. Portfolios — an assessment form that learners do together with their teachers as an alternative to the classic classroom test; the portfolio contains samples of the learner's work and shows growth over time. Tests — a series of questions, problems or physical responses designed to determine knowledge, intelligence or ability. Questionnaires are also used as a tool of assessment.

subjective.question: Differentiate between overt and covert observation, and between participating and non-participating observation.
subjective.answer: Observation can be overt when everyone knows that they are being observed, and covert when nobody knows that they are being observed. The benefit of covert observation is that people behave naturally if they do not know they are being observed; however, overt observations are preferred due to ethical problems. Regarding the role of the observer: in the participating role, the observer takes part in the activity and observes it as well; in the non-participating role, the observer does not take part in the activity and only observes it.

subjective.question: Write the merits and demerits of observation as a tool of assessment.
subjective.answer: Merits of observation: it is direct, independent and natural. Through observation it is possible to discover causes of behaviour, to increase acceptance of individual variations in growth and development, and to interact with others on a more meaningful level. Demerits of observation: observer's bias, effect of the observer on the observed, it is time consuming, and it may give less understanding of the situation.

subjective.question: What is a questionnaire? Describe its different types.
subjective.answer: A questionnaire is a set of printed or written questions with a choice of answers, devised for the purpose of a survey or statistical study. It serves four basic purposes: to collect the appropriate data, to make data comparable for analysis, to minimize bias in formulating and asking the questions, and to make questions engaging. Its types are: open-ended, in which respondents get an opportunity to express their opinions in a free-flowing manner; closed format, in which respondents are restricted to choose among the given multiple choice answers; yes/no format, in which respondents choose positive or negative answers; Likert questions, which ask how strongly respondents agree to a particular statement; bipolar questions, which have two extreme answers written at the opposite ends of a scale; and leading questions, which lead to a particular type of answer. A questionnaire is interpreted through calculations like percentages and making inferences.

subjective.question: Write the merits and demerits of a questionnaire.
subjective.answer: Merits: a questionnaire is practical; a large amount of information can be collected through it; it is easy to manage and easy to analyze; the data is more reliable, more valid and comparable. Demerits: it is inadequate for certain information like the thinking process and behaviour; the questions are the reflection of the person who asks them; there is no way to tell how true the information is; and there is no way to tell how thoughtful the respondent is, as respondents may understand the questions differently.

subjective.question: Differentiate between structured and semi-structured interviews. What do in-depth interviews emphasize?
subjective.answer: A structured interview, or standardized interview, is a method used in survey research whose aim is to confirm that each interview is offered with exactly the same questions in the same order; structured interviews emphasize reliability — how accurately different respondents' answers can be compared. A semi-structured interview is open, allowing new ideas to be brought up during the interview as a result of what the interviewee says. In-depth interviews emphasize validity — how close the answers get to the respondents' real views. The interview is recorded and then transcribed, i.e. a word-to-word written documentation of the taped or live interview is prepared, and the interview is interpreted through this transcription.

subjective.question: Write the merits and demerits of an interview.
subjective.answer: Merits: an interview is practical; it is face to face; the human side is direct; body language can be observed; the interviewee is not influenced by others; the response rate is higher; and there is participation from both sides. Demerits: it is time consuming (setting up, interviewing, transcribing, analyzing, feedback and reporting), it involves cost, and inferences have to be drawn from the transcription.

subjective.question: What is a portfolio? Describe its different types.
subjective.answer: A portfolio is a purposeful collection of a student's work that exhibits the student's efforts, progress and achievements in one or more areas of the curriculum; it helps to get specific information and a record of the progress made by the student in a specific area. Its types are: Project portfolio, which organizes a series of projects into a single portfolio of reports that capture project objectives and other critical factors. Growth portfolio, which organizes a record of the progress made in some specific area, maintaining the record from the starting point to the final stage. Achievement portfolio, which maintains the record of one's achievement in a certain area against specific targets. Competence portfolio, which maintains the record of competition. Process portfolio, which records all phases of the learning process and is particularly useful in documenting students' overall learning. Showcase portfolio, which shows a record of your best achievements throughout the session with the purpose of assessment.

subjective.question: What is reflective writing in diary writing? How are projects assessed, and what are the merits and demerits of projects?
subjective.answer: Diary writing is interpreted as reflective writing: looking back, analyzing the event or idea, and thinking carefully about what the event or idea means; it is considered more personal and provides an opportunity to gain further insights from one's work. A good diary entry includes the date, starts with 'Dear diary', has a first-line summary, a chatty style, is written in the first person and in the past tense. Projects assess a student's understanding of a subject or topic and require students to apply their knowledge and skills while completing the prescribed task; group projects should include a component that each student completes individually. Merits of projects: individualized instruction, self learning and freedom, confidence, self trust, critical thinking, healthy competition with others, helping each other and social interaction. Demerits: time consuming, need of financial resources, problems of control, just focusing on the project, and lack of clarity about assessment.

subjective.question: Describe the different types of tests: diagnostic, standardized, achievement, proficiency and psychometric.
subjective.answer: A test is a procedure used to establish quality, performance or reliability of something — here, the quality of teaching and learning. Diagnostic tests measure students' weaknesses in a subject area or skills; teachers typically administer diagnostic tests for reading and math skills, using the results to provide remedial instruction. A standardized test is any form of test that requires all test takers to answer the same questions, or a selection of questions from a common bank of questions, and that is scored in a standard or consistent manner, which makes it possible to compare performance. An achievement test is a test of skill and knowledge gained in a grade or level, usually through planned instruction such as training or classroom instruction, and achievement is tested against certain objectives. A proficiency test measures a learner's level of language. A psychometric test is an objective and standardized measure of a sample behaviour.

subjective.question: Write short notes on the main objective type questions used in assessment.
subjective.answer: Yes/No questions are simple questions with two possible responses; they allow the rapid assessment of large amounts of material, but there is very little educational benefit in using them. True/False/Not Given questions require the student to analyze a statement and assess whether the information is true, false or not given; they are effective, based on simple logic, and more reliable than yes/no questions. Filling the blanks (close test) is based on simple logic, tests particular/common information and vocabulary, and needs more comprehension. Multiple choice questions consist of one statement with choices; there is a correct answer along with distractors, and students analyze the statement and mark the correct answer. Matching sentences/columns present two lists of words, phrases or sentences and are used for recognition of relationships and making associations across a wide range of subject matter. Objective questions are easy to make and mark and have standardized responses, but they should be written with clarity and clearly communicated.

subjective.question: How are short answer and essay type questions assessed? What precautions are needed?
subjective.answer: Short answer questions require precise and specific information and complete understanding from the student; they can also be covered under the heading of objective questions. Students may often memorize short answer questions with rote learning, so if assessors wish to use them to assess deeper learning, careful attention and much practice on appropriate questions is required. Because these are open-ended questions and students are free to answer in any way they choose, the assessor must be very clear on the type of answers expected when setting the questions; short answer questions can lead to difficulties in grading if the question is not worded carefully. Essay type answers are very common; they require detailed explanation based on information, critical analysis, cause/effect and compare/contrast. While assessing them, the assessor considers the introduction, explanation, critical analysis, cause/effect, compare/contrast, academic writing, coherence, and the summing up and conclusion; answers should follow the general rules of academic writing, with each paragraph beginning with a topic sentence supported by reasons or examples.

subjective.question: Differentiate between an aim and an objective. Why must objectives be aligned with assessment?
subjective.answer: The aims of a course are broad statements of its purpose or intent; the aim encompasses the purpose and philosophy of the course, specifying its overall direction and content, and lets students know what will be taught over a study period. A learning objective is explicit about what the students do and what they need to learn to achieve the aim; objectives may be written with respect to knowledge, skills and attitudes. The principal difference is that aims represent the broad goal of the course while objectives are the steps the students need to take in order to get there. For an objective to be claimed, it must be assessed; therefore there must be an alignment between objectives and assessments. Assessment allows the instructor to check the degree to which students are meeting the learning objectives, and assessment must align with the instructional techniques, otherwise the objectives will not be attained. For example, if teaching is about definitions, the assessment should be 'Define so and so…'; teaching definitions but assessing through 'Explain…' is a mismatch between teaching and assessment.

subjective.question: What is Bloom's Taxonomy? Describe its three domains and its significance for assessment.
subjective.answer: Taxonomy is the science of classification according to a predetermined system. Bloom's Taxonomy was created in 1956 under the leadership of educational psychologist Dr Benjamin Bloom in order to promote higher forms of thinking in education, such as analyzing and evaluating concepts, processes, procedures and principles, rather than just remembering facts (rote learning). It is most often used when designing instruction or learning processes, as it makes one clear about the level and depth of the learning process, and it is helpful in writing objectives and then in forming questions. Its three domains are: Cognitive — mental skills (knowledge); Affective — growth in feelings or emotional areas (attitude or self); and Psychomotor — manual or physical skills (skills). These domains are referred to as KSA (Knowledge, Skills, Attitudes/Abilities), and after a learning activity the learner should have acquired a new skill, knowledge and attitude. In the revised taxonomy, the names of the six major categories of the cognitive domain were changed from noun to verb forms, Comprehension and Synthesis were retitled as Understanding and Creating, and the two top levels, Evaluation and Synthesis, were interchanged.

subjective.topic: The Cognitive Levels of Bloom's Taxonomy
subjective.question: Describe the Knowledge and Comprehension levels of Bloom's Taxonomy with their verbs, objectives and questions.
subjective.answer: Knowledge level: the student exhibits previously learned material by recalling facts, terms, basic concepts and answers; it refers to rote memorization of facts and information. Its related verbs and words include arrange, define, describe, duplicate, identify, label, list, match, memorize, name, outline, recognize, recall, repeat, reproduce, state, who, what and when. Knowledge level objectives are like 'Students will be able to define nouns', and its questions test rote memorization, e.g. 'What is a noun?' A mismatch occurs when the objective is 'define noun' but the question asks to 'explain the function of noun in a paragraph'. Comprehension level: the student demonstrates understanding of facts and ideas by organizing, comparing, translating, interpreting, giving descriptions and stating main ideas; in short, grasping the meaning of information. Its verbs include demonstrate, interpret, explain, extend, illustrate, infer, outline, relate, rephrase, translate, summarize, show and classify. At this level the learner can restate in his own words what he has stored in memory, e.g. objective 'Students will be able to explain the theory' and question 'How does global warming affect us?'

subjective.topic: The Cognitive Levels of Bloom's Taxonomy
subjective.question: Describe the Application, Analysis, Synthesis and Evaluation levels of Bloom's Taxonomy.
subjective.answer: Application level refers to applying gained knowledge to actual situations; the student solves problems by applying acquired knowledge, facts, techniques and rules. Its verbs include apply, build, construct, develop, make use of, organize, solve, utilize and model; e.g. 'Solve the following problem.' Analysis level means examining and breaking information into parts by identifying motives or causes, making inferences and finding evidence to support generalizations; it is breaking down objects or ideas into simpler parts and seeing how the parts relate and are organized. Its verbs include analyze, categorize, classify, compare, contrast, discover, divide, examine and inspect; e.g. 'Distinguish between hard disc and removable disc.' Synthesis level refers to compiling information together by combining elements in a new pattern or proposing alternative solutions. Its verbs include combine, compile, compose, construct, create, design, develop, formulate, invent, originate and plan; e.g. 'How will you design your classroom for language learning activities?' Evaluation level refers to making judgments about information, validity of ideas or quality of work based on a set of criteria. Its verbs include criticize, decide, defend, evaluate, judge, justify, compare, rate, recommend, appraise and support; e.g. 'How will you justify the educational reforms?' Objectives and questions at each level must be of the same level; otherwise there is a mismatch between objectives and questions.
